questions.q: What is a threat model, in the context of a robustness evaluation, and when should it be written?
options: A list of every known CVE affecting the model's serving infrastructure
A record of the model's training hyperparameters and dataset version
A diagram of the neural network's layer architecture
A written statement of the attacker's goal, knowledge, capability, and access, decided before any attack is run
questions.explain: A threat model defines goal, knowledge, capability, and access up front; without it, a robustness number can't be interpreted because you don't know what risk it was actually measuring.

questions.q: Why is evaluating a defense with a single weak attack like plain FGSM not trustworthy on its own?
options: Weak attacks always take longer to run than strong attacks
A defense that only survives a weak attack may just be breaking that attack's assumptions (obfuscated gradients) without closing the real vulnerability
Weak attacks cannot be implemented in open-source libraries
A weak attack always produces a higher attack success rate than a strong one
questions.explain: Surviving one weak attack can reflect obfuscated gradients rather than genuine robustness — the exact failure pattern documented across multiple published defenses.

questions.q: What is an adaptive attack, and why does a credible evaluation require one?
options: An attack that automatically patches the model's vulnerability once it succeeds
An attack that only works against models deployed on cloud infrastructure
An attack built with full knowledge of a specific defense mechanism, used specifically to try to defeat it
An attack that requires no computational resources to execute
questions.explain: A defense that only survives attacks that don't know it exists hasn't really been tested; an adaptive attack is designed with the defense's mechanism in mind.

questions.q: What tooling do security and ML teams actually use for structured, reproducible robustness evaluation?
options: IBM's Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART), CleverHans, and Foolbox — established open-source libraries implementing standard attacks for reproducible evaluation
Only proprietary, closed-source tools can be used for a credible robustness evaluation
A standard antivirus engine, since it already tests for malware evasion
A spreadsheet tracking manually guessed perturbations
questions.explain: ART, CleverHans, and Foolbox are established open-source libraries that implement standard attacks like FGSM and PGD consistently, making evaluations reproducible and comparable across teams.

questions.q: What does a usable robustness evaluation report need to state, at minimum?
options: Only whether the model passed or failed, with no supporting numbers
Clean accuracy, robust accuracy at a specified attack and perturbation budget, and attack success rate — never report robust accuracy without naming the attack and budget
The model's total parameter count and training duration
The name of the engineer who trained the model
questions.explain: A 'robust accuracy' figure is meaningless without naming the attack and the perturbation budget it was measured under, alongside the clean-accuracy baseline and attack success rate.
